title: Question 3
stem:
A ball of mass $150\text{ g}$ is at rest on a horizontal floor, as shown in Fig. 3.1.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the normal contact force from the floor acting on the ball.
hints: Hint 1: The ball is sitting still on the floor, so think about the downward pull on it and remember to convert the 150 g mass into kilograms first.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the forces at rest**
You have a ball just sitting on the floor. Gravity pulls it down with its weight, and the floor pushes back up with a normal contact force. Because it is not moving, those two must balance.

Step 2: **Calculate the weight**
Convert mass to kilograms: $$m = 150 \text{ g} = 0.150 \text{ kg}$$ Then weight is: $$W = mg = 0.150 \times 9.81 = 1.47 \text{ N}$$ Since the forces balance, the normal contact force has this same magnitude, $1.47 \text{ N}$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: resultant force (on ball) is zero so normal contact force = weight or the forces are in opposite directions so normal contact force = weight or normal contact force up = weight down

hints: Hint 1: Think about what the total or resultant force must be when an object stays at rest with no acceleration.
parts.proper_answer: The ball is in equilibrium so resultant force is zero, therefore upward normal contact force equals downward weight in magnitude.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the idea of equilibrium**
At rest means velocity is zero and stays zero, so acceleration is zero. By Newton's first law, the resultant force on the ball must be zero.

Step 2: **Balance up and down**
The only vertical forces are weight down and normal contact force up. For their vector sum to be zero they must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. That is why your calculation in (i) works.

parts.label: (b)
(b)(i)
parts.text: State Newton's second law of motion.

markscheme_points.text: (resultant) force proportional/equal to rate of change of momentum

hints: Hint 1: Think about linking resultant force not to momentum itself, but to how fast that momentum is changing with time.
parts.proper_answer: The resultant force acting on a body is proportional (equal) to the rate of change of momentum of the body.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **State the momentum form**
Newton's second law is most generally written with momentum, not just $F = ma$. It says: $$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$ in words, resultant force equals rate of change of momentum. The direction of the force is the same as the direction of the change in momentum.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the average resultant force on the ball when it is in contact with the floor.
hints: Hint 1: Take upward as positive and think carefully about the signs of the velocity just before contact (down) and just after contact (up).
Hint 2: Think about how to combine the 6.2 and 2.5 values to get the total change in velocity, and what you multiply by to turn that into momentum change.
Hint 3: Think about how the contact time of 0.12 s links that momentum change to the average force, and which way the force must push to reverse the motion.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the change in momentum**
Momentum is a vector, so direction matters. Let upward be positive. Then $v_{initial} = -6.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $v_{final} = +2.5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Change in velocity is: $$\Delta v = v_{final} - v_{initial} = 2.5 - (-6.2) = 8.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$ upwards. Multiply by mass in kg: $$\Delta p = m\Delta v = 0.150 \times 8.7 = 1.305 \text{ N s}$$

Step 2: **Divide by time for average force**
From Newton's second law: $$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{1.305}{0.12} = 10.9 \text{ N}$$ Rounded to 2 s.f., this is about $11 \text{ N}$. This is the average resultant force on the ball during contact.

Step 3: **Give the direction**
The momentum change is upwards, from down to up, so the resultant force causing it must also be upwards. The floor pushes up harder than gravity during the short impact to reverse the ball's motion.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: State and explain whether linear momentum is conserved during the collision of the ball with the floor.

markscheme_points.text: there is a change/gain in momentum of the floor
this is equal (and opposite) to the change/loss in momentum of the ball so momentum is conserved
or change of (total) momentum of ball and floor is zero
or (total) momentum of ball and floor before is equal to the (total) momentum of ball and floor after

hints: Hint 1: Think about whether you are considering the ball on its own or the ball together with the floor and Earth as one combined system.
Hint 2: Think about where the momentum apparently lost by the ball must have gone if no external force acts on that combined system.
parts.proper_answer: Yes, linear momentum is conserved for the ball-floor (Earth) system. The change in momentum of the ball is equal and opposite to the change in momentum of the floor, so total momentum change is zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Look at the ball alone versus the whole system**
If you look only at the ball, its momentum clearly changes from downwards to upwards, so it looks like momentum is not conserved. That is because the floor exerts an external force on the ball during contact.

Step 2: **Include the floor to conserve momentum**
Now include the floor plus Earth as part of the system. The ball pushes down on the floor while the floor pushes up on the ball. The floor gains downward momentum exactly equal in size to the upward momentum change of the ball. So: $$\Delta p_{total} = \Delta p_{ball} + \Delta p_{floor} = 0$$ Total momentum before equals total momentum after, so linear momentum is conserved for the combined system.
